title: Maitreyi's question
hook: Nani says the line by heart, and why the tradition puts hearing first
carry: shruti: the holy word is heard first
tomorrow: after the card, Nani has one note for Priya. what is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, om: the one sound for brahman of speech and a line to keep: speech is tapas, true, kind and helpful, all at once, the way Hanuman spoke to Rama. Today, one question.

A grandmother opens a birthday card and finds a line from the Gita written inside, in careful, slightly wobbly Devanagari. She glances at it and doesn't read it. She says it, the whole verse, by heart, eyes on her granddaughter instead of the page. She learned it the way she learned her first songs: by ear, long before she read it. Which raises today's question: why does this tradition put hearing first?
screen: `A CARD, A LINE OF THE GITA.` → `SHE SAYS IT BY HEART.` → `WHY PUT HEARING FIRST?`

segments.voice: Start with a name. Hindus call the Vedas shruti, what is heard: tradition says seers heard them, and teachers handed them on mouth to ear, keeping every sound. And there's a story about what that hearing is for. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya is about to leave home for the life of a renunciant, and offers to divide what he owns between his two wives. One of them, Maitreyi, asks him: if this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like any rich person's life. Then what would I do with it, she says. Tell me what you know. So he does. The Self, he tells her, is what should be seen; and the way there is hearing, then reflecting, then meditating. Hearing comes first. Now a neighbor that also begins with the ear. In Judaism, a line from Deuteronomy is said morning and evening, the Shema: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Shared: two old traditions that open with listening, not looking. And an honest difference. The Shema declares the one God, and the Torah is read from a scroll written by hand, every letter kept. The Vedas, tradition says, were carried by voice, every sound kept. Both are ways of listening closely enough that a holy word isn't lost.
screen: `SHRUTI: WHAT IS HEARD.` · `WOULD WEALTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` · `HEAR, THEN REFLECT, THEN MEDITATE.` · `THE SHEMA: HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `ONE KEEPS THE LETTER, ONE THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: With eyes open or closed, listen to the farthest sound you can hear, then the nearest, then your own breath. Don't name them; just hear them, the way a student hears a teacher's line before saying it back. When the mind starts talking, go back to listening.
The sounds: in a tradition that calls the Vedas shruti, what is heard, the ear comes before the eye.
Hold on to it: shruti, the holy word is heard first, and the reading follows after. See you tomorrow.

shruti.meaning: what is heard; the name for the Vedas

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.1–2.4.5 (Maitreyi's question; the Self to be seen, heard, reflected on, meditated on)

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): shared with Judaism, in its own words (Deuteronomy 6:4, JPS 1917): hearing first. Honest difference: the Shema declares the one God and is read from a handwritten Torah scroll, keeping every letter; the Vedas, tradition says, were carried by voice, keeping every sound. Neither ranked; no 'all the same'.

Brihadaranyaka 2.4.5 (ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ): paraphrased as the Self should be seen, and the way is hearing, reflecting, meditating. Shravana-manana-nididhyasana as three steps is the later Vedanta reading, named only in the trapdoor. Confirm.

'Said morning and evening' (the Shema) follows Deuteronomy 6:7 and Jewish practice; confirm phrasing. The Gita is not itself shruti (it is usually classed as smriti); the lesson keeps shruti for the Vedas and has Nani know the Gita line by ear.

Gloss 'Vedas' says 'the oldest Hindu scriptures': soften to 'the Hindu scriptures called shruti' if the Keeper prefers. Priya storyline: Nani's birthday; Sam has mended things with Priya and is there (the chat stays on the card).
